stages.name: Game theory and pricing behaviour
stages.title: Game theory and pricing behaviour
stages.sub: How firms' interdependent choices lead to stable but sometimes jointly worse outcomes, and how price competition can turn destructive.

steps.q: Two petrol stations set prices without knowing what the other will do. Station A works out that cutting its price gives it more profit whether Station B cuts its price or not. What kind of choice is 'cut price' for Station A?
steps.right: The best choice no matter what B does
steps.wrong: Only the best choice if B also cuts
steps.hint: The question says A comes out ahead whichever way B moves.

steps.q: Both stations end up cutting price, since each finds it best regardless of the other. Once there, would either gain by switching back to a high price on its own?
steps.right: No, switching alone would make it worse off
steps.wrong: Yes, switching alone would make it better off
steps.hint: If A alone raised its price while B stayed low, would A win back custom or lose it to B's lower price?

steps.q: If both stations had instead agreed to keep prices high, both would have earned more profit than they do now with both cutting. So does each firm reaching its own best individual choice lead to the best joint outcome?
steps.right: No, both end up worse off than if they had kept prices high
steps.wrong: Yes, individually best choices also give the best joint result
steps.hint: Compare total profits: both high, versus both cut.

steps.q: Firms distrust each other, or competition law bans agreements, so instead of co-operating on price they keep cutting to undercut each other, and each cut is met with a further cut. What is happening to prices?
steps.right: They keep falling in repeated rounds of cuts
steps.wrong: They settle quickly at one lower level

steps.q: One large firm in this price-cutting battle can afford to sell for a while at a price below its own costs, something its smaller rivals cannot survive for long. Why would it deliberately price below cost?
steps.right: To force weaker rivals out or scare off new entrants
steps.wrong: To maximise its own short-run profit
steps.hint: Selling below cost loses money now; what longer-term market position does that buy the large firm?
